title: ANA by HEp-2 Immunofluorescence: Patterns, DFS70 and Negative Results
summary: Interpret HEp-2 IIFA ANA results by titre and ICAP pattern, choose the pattern-directed follow-up antibody, understand when anti-DFS70 is reassuring, and know why a negative ANA does not exclude every systemic autoimmune disease.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 53 Hits 2 and 10 and Traps 1 and 4 (first lesson for Ch. 53). Checked against Damoiseaux 2019 (ICAP clinical relevance) and Cheng 2021 (anti-DFS70 meta-analysis). Not taught: the reviewer’s specific list of antibodies that HEp-2 IFA misses (Ro60, Ro52, La, Ku, RNA polymerases, PM/Scl) — the sources read support only the general statement that AC-0 occurs in SARD and that some anti-synthetases give no pattern; WHO reporting at 1:40 and 1:160 (Hit 12; Agmon-Levin 2014 not accessible).

objectives: Describe the HEp-2 IIFA and ICAP pattern coding.
Choose follow-up tests from the ANA pattern.
Interpret anti-DFS70 and negative ANA results correctly.

scenes.title: Positive ANA, negative ANA — both misleading?
scenes.altText: Two invented HEp-2 reports. Patient 1: healthy 30-year-old with fatigue, ANA positive 1:640, dense fine speckled pattern (AC-2). Patient 2: progressive muscle weakness, interstitial lung disease, “mechanic’s hands” — HEp-2 IIFA negative (AC-0). Question token: “Does the first have lupus? Does the second have no autoimmune disease?”

cues.text: A healthy 30-year-old with fatigue has a strongly positive ANA, 1 in 640, with a dense fine speckled pattern.
Another patient has progressive muscle weakness, interstitial lung disease and cracked “mechanic’s hands”, but the ANA test is negative.
Does the first patient have lupus? Does the second have no autoimmune disease?

scenes.title: What the HEp-2 IIFA shows
scenes.altText: Method card (ICAP, Damoiseaux 2019): indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells is the gold standard screening test for autoantibodies in systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARD). The test gives more than positive/negative: an antibody level (titre) and a pattern, coded AC-0 (negative) to AC-29 by the International Consensus on ANA Patterns (ICAP). Schematic: homogeneous (AC-1), dense fine speckled (AC-2), centromere (AC-3), fine speckled (AC-20).

cues.text: The screening test is indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells, reinforced as the gold standard for autoantibody screening in systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases.
Antibodies in the patient’s serum that bind cellular antigens are made visible by immunofluorescence, so the test shows where in the cell they bind.
The result is more than yes or no. It gives a titre and a staining pattern, coded by the International Consensus on ANA Patterns, from AC-0, negative, upward.
Patterns include homogeneous, AC-1; dense fine speckled, AC-2; centromere, AC-3; and fine speckled, AC-20.

scenes.title: Pattern points to the follow-up test
scenes.altText: Follow-up card (ICAP 2019): AC-1 homogeneous — found in SLE, chronic autoimmune hepatitis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis; if SLE is suspected, test anti-dsDNA (± nucleosome/chromatin). AC-3 centromere — common in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. AC-20 fine speckled — if Sjögren syndrome, SLE, subacute cutaneous or neonatal lupus, or congenital heart block is suspected, test anti-SS-A/Ro (Ro60) and anti-SS-B/La; AC-20 is also reported with anti-Jo-1 (follow up with anti-Jo-1). AC-2 dense fine speckled — negative association with SARD only if confirmed as anti-DFS70 (LEDGF/p75) and no other common ENA is present; AC-2 can be caused by other antibodies; confirmatory DFS70 assays may be available only in specialty laboratories. Meta-analysis (Cheng 2021, 8 studies, 4,168 ANA-positive patients): anti-DFS70 for excluding SARD — sensitivity 0.19, specificity 0.93.

cues.text: The pattern guides the next test. Homogeneous, AC-1, occurs in lupus, autoimmune hepatitis and juvenile arthritis; if lupus is suspected, test anti-double-stranded DNA.

Centromere, AC-3, is common in limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis. Fine speckled, AC-20, prompts anti-SS-A/Ro and anti-SS-B/La when Sjögren syndrome or lupus is suspected, and anti-Jo-1 when myositis is.

Dense fine speckled, AC-2, argues against a systemic autoimmune disease, but only if the antibody is confirmed as anti-DFS70 and no other disease antibody is present. Other antibodies can mimic the pattern.
In a 2021 meta-analysis of 4,168 ANA-positive patients, anti-DFS70 had a specificity of 93 percent but a sensitivity of only 19 percent for the absence of a systemic autoimmune disease.

scenes.title: When a negative ANA is not the end
scenes.altText: Limitation card (ICAP 2019): clinicians should be aware of clinical suspicion and order specific tests accordingly, anticipating HEp-2 IIFA-negative (AC-0) results in SARD. Not all anti-tRNA synthetase antibodies produce a HEp-2 pattern; only some anti-Jo-1 give AC-20, others (EJ, KS, OJ, PL-7, PL-12) more often AC-19. Disease-specific immunoassays (myositis, systemic sclerosis, autoimmune liver profiles) are often only available in specialty laboratories. Back to the hook: Patient 1 — AC-2 high titre: confirm anti-DFS70; if mono-specific with no other ENA, SARD is less likely (not proven absent). Patient 2 — clinical picture of antisynthetase syndrome with AC-0: order a myositis profile (anti-Jo-1 and other anti-synthetases) despite the negative ANA.

cues.text: A negative ANA does not end the work-up when the clinical picture fits. The consensus warns that negative HEp-2 results occur in systemic autoimmune disease.
For example, not all antibodies to transfer-RNA synthetases produce a HEp-2 pattern, and only some anti-Jo-1 antibodies give the fine speckled pattern.
So when myositis with lung disease is suspected, order the specific antibodies, often in a myositis profile from a specialty laboratory.
Back to patient one: confirm anti-DFS70. If it is the only antibody, a systemic autoimmune disease is less likely, though not excluded.
Patient two: despite the negative ANA, order anti-Jo-1 and the other anti-synthetase antibodies.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A negative ANA rules out SARD” (✓ AC-0 occurs in SARD; order specific antibodies if suspicion is high); “Any high-titre ANA means lupus” (✓ the pattern matters — confirmed mono-specific anti-DFS70 argues against SARD); “All ANA patterns are clinically equal” (✓ each ICAP pattern points to a specific follow-up test).

cues.text: Trap one: a negative ANA rules out systemic autoimmune disease. No: negative HEp-2 results occur in these diseases; order specific antibodies when suspicion is high.
Trap two: any high-titre ANA means lupus. No: a confirmed mono-specific anti-DFS70 antibody argues against a systemic autoimmune disease.
Trap three: all ANA patterns mean the same. No: each pattern points to a different follow-up test.

props.title: ✗ “Negative ANA rules out SARD.”
lines: ✓ AC-0 occurs in SARD → specific tests

scenes.title: The pattern is the referral letter
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “The ANA pattern is a referral letter — it tells you which specialist test to call.” Tokens: Homogeneous → dsDNA · Fine speckled → Ro/La/Jo-1 · Dense fine speckled → DFS70 (reassuring if alone) · Negative + strong suspicion → order anyway. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: the ANA pattern is a referral letter. Homogeneous refers you to anti-dsDNA; fine speckled to Ro, La or Jo-1; dense fine speckled to anti-DFS70, reassuring if alone. And a negative ANA with strong suspicion still gets specific tests.
Where it breaks: patterns can be mixed or hard to distinguish, such as AC-2 versus AC-20; patterns are not specific for one antibody; and solid-phase ANA assays do not give patterns at all.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “HEp-2 IIFA = gold-standard screen · titre + ICAP pattern · pattern → follow-up (AC-1 dsDNA, AC-20 Ro/La/Jo-1)”, “AC-0 occurs in SARD → order specific antibodies · mono-specific anti-DFS70 argues against SARD (spec 0.93, sens 0.19)”.

cues.text: Read an ANA by titre and ICAP pattern, use the pattern to choose the follow-up test, treat a confirmed mono-specific anti-DFS70 as reassuring, and never let a negative HEp-2 result stop testing when the clinical picture fits.

props.label: HEp-2 IIFA: titre + pattern · AC-1 → dsDNA · AC-20 → Ro/La/Jo-1
AC-0 in SARD → specific tests · DFS70 alone argues against SARD

explanation.what: Plain language: the ANA test looks for antibodies against the cell nucleus by letting patient serum stain cultured cells; how strongly and in what pattern they light up hints at which disease-linked antibody to test next, and some harmless antibodies and some disease antibodies do not behave as expected. Scientific terms: antinuclear antibody (ANA), indirect immunofluorescence assay (IIFA), HEp-2 cells, titre, ICAP pattern (AC codes), extractable nuclear antigens (ENA), anti-dsDNA, anti-SS-A/Ro, anti-SS-B/La, anti-Jo-1, anti-DFS70 (LEDGF/p75), systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease (SARD).
explanation.why: Different autoantigens sit in different cellular compartments, so antibodies against them produce characteristic staining patterns. Antigen distribution and assay design mean some disease antibodies give no HEp-2 staining, while antibodies to DFS70 are common in people without SARD.
explanation.measure: ICAP (Damoiseaux 2019): HEp-2 IIFA gold-standard screen; titre and pattern; AC-1 → anti-dsDNA if SLE suspected; AC-3 → limited cutaneous SSc; AC-20 → anti-SS-A/Ro60 and SS-B/La (SjS, SLE, SCLE, neonatal lupus, congenital heart block) and anti-Jo-1; AC-2 → anti-DFS70 confirmation, negative association only if confirmed and no other ENA; AC-0 occurs in SARD; not all anti-tRNA synthetases give a pattern. Cheng 2021: anti-DFS70 specificity 0.93, sensitivity 0.19 for absence of SARD.
explanation.differs: Mono-specific anti-DFS70 (argues against SARD) vs disease-associated antibodies (point toward SARD); IIFA screening (pattern, titre) vs specific immunoassays (single antigens).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the ANA screening method, which follow-up test a pattern suggests, the meaning of anti-DFS70, and whether a negative ANA excludes disease.

questions.stem: An ANA by HEp-2 IIFA shows a homogeneous (AC-1) pattern in a patient with suspected SLE. Which follow-up test is recommended?

options.rationale: Correct. ICAP recommends anti-dsDNA (± nucleosome) follow-up when AC-1 is seen and SLE is suspected.
Incorrect. Anti-DFS70 confirmation is for the dense fine speckled (AC-2) pattern.
Incorrect. Centromere antibodies give the AC-3 pattern.
Incorrect. AC-1 also occurs in autoimmune hepatitis and JIA; specific antibodies are needed.

questions.stem: A patient with a high-titre AC-2 (dense fine speckled) ANA has confirmed anti-DFS70 antibodies and no other ENA antibodies. How should this be interpreted?

options.text: It argues against a systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease, without excluding it
options.rationale: Correct. Confirmed mono-specific anti-DFS70 is negatively associated with SARD (specificity ~0.93).
Incorrect. Anti-DFS70 is common in people without SARD.
Incorrect. Sjögren syndrome is associated with anti-SS-A/Ro and SS-B/La.

options.text: It means the ANA was a technical error
options.rationale: Incorrect. The antibody is real; it is simply not disease-associated in this setting.

questions.stem: A patient with myositis, interstitial lung disease and mechanic’s hands has a negative HEp-2 IIFA (AC-0). What is the best next step?

options.text: Order specific myositis antibodies, including anti-Jo-1 and other anti-synthetases
options.rationale: Correct. Not all anti-tRNA synthetase antibodies produce a HEp-2 pattern; order tests based on clinical suspicion.
Incorrect. AC-0 results occur in SARD.

options.text: Repeat the ANA in 6 months only
options.rationale: Incorrect. Specific antibody testing is indicated now.
Incorrect. Anti-DFS70 relates to the AC-2 pattern and does not address myositis.
